profile.name: Shai Hope
profile.writeup:
There is a certain neatness to a team turning to a player named Hope whenever things look difficult, and West Indies cricket has leaned on that coincidence more than once over the past decade. Whether chasing a daunting target, steadying a wobbling top order, or simply needing someone dependable at the crease, Shai Hope has spent his career quietly becoming exactly what his name suggests, the man West Indies turn to when they need something to believe in.


Born in Saint Michael, Barbados, Hope made his first-class debut in the 2012-13 season and spent the next few years working his way up through regional cricket. A breakout 2014-15 campaign confirmed he was ready for higher honours, and he backed it up the following season with another prolific run. In March 2017, he brought up his maiden first-class double-century at his home ground, Kensington Oval, a fitting milestone for a batter who had already made his Test debut for West Indies two years earlier, in 2015.


His ODI career began in 2016, in a tri-series alongside Zimbabwe and Sri Lanka, and he announced himself almost immediately, scoring his maiden ODI hundred in just his second appearance in the format. It was in Test cricket, though, that he produced his most celebrated individual performance. Against England at Headingley in 2017, Hope scored twin centuries in the same match, guiding his side to a famous win while chasing 322. His efforts earned him the Player of the Match award and a wave of recognition back home.


The following year, he swept Cricket West Indies' annual honours, named Men's Cricketer of the Year, Test Cricketer of the Year and ODI Cricketer of the Year in the same ceremony, before being named ODI Player of the Year again in 2019. That same year brought one of the most remarkable performances of his career, as he and opening partner John Campbell put together a world-record 365-run opening stand in an ODI against Ireland. The innings also pushed Hope past 3,000 ODI runs faster than any West Indian before him.


His Test form, however, faded over the following seasons, and he was dropped from the format entirely in 2021. His white-ball game barely missed a beat in response. He continued to rack up landmark after landmark in ODI cricket, eventually matching Viv Richards as the joint-fastest West Indian to reach 5,000 ODI runs, and was named in the ICC's ODI Team of the Year for 2022. By 2023, Hope's consistency and composure had made him the obvious choice to lead West Indies in white-ball cricket, first taking over the ODI captaincy before the role expanded to cover T20Is as well.


That standing in the side eventually earned him a recall to Test cricket too, nearly four years after his last appearance, when he was brought back for West Indies' home series against Australia in June 2025 at the start of a new World Test Championship cycle. He went on to play a full role across formats through 2026, including further Test appearances, ODI and T20I series, and a prominent part in West Indies' campaign at that year's T20 World Cup.


Alongside his national duties, Hope has built a wide-ranging franchise career, most notably in the Caribbean Premier League. He has represented Guyana Amazon Warriors since 2022, won the title with them in 2023, and finished as the tournament's leading run-scorer in 2025. Across more than a decade in the game, Hope has established himself among the most consistent ODI run-scorers of his era, and his name has become synonymous with a calm head whenever West Indies have needed one most.
